title: Texas Has a Theory of Education
author: The Next 30 Years
summary: This article examines the Texas State Board of Education's adoption of new social studies standards as an expression of a coherent, knowledge-building educational philosophy — not merely a political intervention, but a pedagogical one. The author argues that Texas, alone among states, has developed a recognizable theory of how students acquire knowledge: that factual content and vocabulary are the vehicle of literacy, that knowledge is cumulative (you can only comprehend what you already know something about), and that a well-sequenced curriculum is therefore a literacy curriculum. Drawing on Natalie Wexler's work and the broader knowledge-rich curriculum movement, the article traces how the Texas standards embody these principles through specific reading lists and content requirements. The piece distinguishes between curriculum as a compliance exercise and curriculum as a theory of mind, suggesting that most states approach standards from the former orientation while Texas has (perhaps unwittingly) landed on the latter. The article is valuable to educators and policymakers who want to understand what it actually means for a state to have a 'theory of education' rather than a list of requirements.
points: Texas's standards implicitly encode the knowledge-rich curriculum argument — that comprehension depends on prior knowledge, and therefore content is not separable from literacy instruction — even if the framers would not use that theoretical language.

The article's key distinction is between curriculum as compliance (what students should be able to do) and curriculum as theory of mind (what students need to know to be able to think); most states operate from the former, Texas from something closer to the latter.

Natalie Wexler's argument that knowledge is cumulative — you can only understand what you already have schemas to attach new information to — is the intellectual backbone of the Texas approach, even if never cited explicitly.

A well-sequenced content curriculum is simultaneously a literacy curriculum: when students acquire world knowledge systematically, their reading comprehension grows as a byproduct because they have context for what they read.
The piece suggests that the political controversy over what is in Texas standards obscures the more interesting pedagogical question of what theory of learning underlies the choices being made.
quotes: This June, the Texas State Board of Education adopted [ ] new social studies standards and a required literature reading list for its public schools. These changes follow Texas’s 2024 release [ ] of its “Bluebonnet” curriculum, a package of instructional resources for elementary school, which sparked controversy over the inclusion of Bible stories in the reading materials.

The standards explicitly call for concepts to be embedded in stories and historical content in order to “create schema for understanding.” This is a significant departure from the way American education often thinks about social studies—and education more broadly. For decades, schools have been encouraged to focus on skills: critical thinking, problem solving, analysis, collaboration, and, in literacy, comprehension strategies such as finding the main idea, making inferences, and identifying the author’s purpose.

A school system cannot be indifferent to whether one classroom studies ancient Egypt, another spends six weeks on a generic unit about “communities,” and a third pursues student-selected projects, and then assume all children will arrive at the next grade equally prepared. Natalie Wexler, one of the nation’s most important advocates for knowledge-building curriculum, recently praised [ ] the ambition and specificity of the Texas social studies standards while worrying that their perceived ideological coloration could unnecessarily inflame the culture wars.
That question does not yield an immutable list of names, books, and events. Speech communities change, and America’s cultural inheritance has always expanded and evolved [ ].

It should not be controversial for them to cultivate some measure of affection for the community, state, and country that created and sustains them. This need not require triumphalism, mythology, or silence about injustice.

The Texas social studies standards are admirably explicit about this knowledge-building component of civics. They aim to develop responsible citizens who understand constitutional government, consent of the governed, civic virtue, individual rights, and the preservation of liberty.

Texas plans to align its reading assessments with its knowledge-building ambitions, drawing some passages from the literary works list and others from content students will have studied in science and social studies. If schools know that reading comprehension will be tested partly through material students are supposed to have encountered, the familiar dictum that “what gets tested gets taught” may finally be put to constructive purpose.
